splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on when actuarial assumptions must be finalized for calculating employer withdrawal liability from multiemployer pension plans under ERISA. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers because the timing of assumption selection directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about the limits of judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during the period a supervisee is a fugitive, allowing courts to revoke supervised release even after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled by absconding because no statutory provision authorizes such tolling, and the term expires as stated in the judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing successive motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1)—which prohibits raising any claim previously presented—when bringing successive § 2255 motions. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are barred from raising previously presented claims in addition to the separate requirements of § 2255(h). If it does not apply, prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the § 2244(b)(1) bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to successive § 2255 motions because § 2255(h) provides its own gatekeeping criteria for federal prisoners, making the additional bar inapplicable.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting rules. The outcome determines whether election administration disputes can be litigated before an election or must wait until after, raising profound practical concerns about the timing of judicial review of election procedures.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office have Article III standing to challenge state election laws before an election based on competitive injury or vote-dilution theories.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate does not have Article III standing to challenge state ballot-counting rules pre-election because the alleged injury is too speculative or generalized.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes priority over agency or Sentencing Commission deference (formerly Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether lenity trumps deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous criminal provisions. At least three circuits hold that lenity prevails over deference, while others (including the Third Circuit) have held that deference trumps lenity. This split has deepened after Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo overruled Chevron deference.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity prevails over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal or sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through delegated power.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes priority over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous guidelines enhancements or criminal provisions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision means 'and' or 'or.' This determines whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria to be disqualified from safety-valve relief or whether possessing any one is sufficient. The split leads to dramatically different sentences for identically situated defendants depending on geographic location.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its natural conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as distributive or disjunctive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Commission's Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is entitled to deference when the guideline text does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy and other inchoate offenses in the definition of 'controlled substance offense' for career-offender purposes is a valid interpretation of the guideline text or impermissibly expands the guideline beyond its plain language. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders under the Guidelines.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is a permissible interpretation of the ambiguous guideline text and that inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is not entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' beyond what the text allows.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state law criminalizes a substance not listed on the federal controlled substances schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally controlled. Some circuits hold that any state drug offense qualifies regardless of whether the substance is federally scheduled, while others require a match with federal schedules. This affects defendants' base offense levels and career-offender status.

positions.label: No federal-match requirement
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a controlled substance offense under the Guidelines even if the substance is not controlled under federal law, because the guideline text refers to 'state law' offenses without limitation.

positions.label: Federal-match requirement applies
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction must involve a substance also controlled under federal law to qualify as a controlled substance offense under the Guidelines, requiring a categorical match.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether non-retroactive changes in law, particularly the First Step Act's elimination of mandatory consecutive 'stacked' § 924(c) sentences, can serve as a basis for compassionate release. Some circuits categorically bar consideration of such changes, while others allow them as one factor. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment attempted to resolve this, but circuits disagree on its validity.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law may be considered as one factor among others in evaluating whether extraordinary and compelling reasons warrant a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the civil timeline (30 days under FRAP 4(a)) or the criminal timeline (14 days under FRAP 4(b)).
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil or criminal matter for purposes of determining the appellate deadline. The majority view treats it as civil (30-day deadline), while at least one circuit applies the criminal timeline (14-day deadline). This procedural question determines whether many appeals are timely filed.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies (30 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies (14 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, so the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions affecting the terms (but not necessarily the fact or duration) of imprisonment must proceed via habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or may bring claims under other statutory vehicles such as Bivens or the APA.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for federal prisoners challenging BOP decisions that affect the execution of their sentences but do not directly challenge the fact or duration of confinement. This affects prisoners challenging BOP policies on earned time credits, halfway house placements, and other administrative decisions under the First Step Act.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for challenges to execution of sentence
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the execution of a sentence, including transfer to prerelease custody, must be brought under the habeas statutes as the exclusive federal remedy.

positions.label: Other remedies available for conditions-of-confinement claims
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring non-habeas claims (e.g., Bivens, § 1983, or APA actions) to challenge conditions of confinement or BOP administrative decisions that do not directly affect the duration of imprisonment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity of a debtor's assets become property of the bankruptcy estate when a Chapter 13 case is converted in good faith to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in asset value that occurs between the original Chapter 13 filing and subsequent conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the bankruptcy estate or the debtor. This question directly affects how much equity is available to creditors in converted bankruptcy cases and the financial consequences of conversion for debtors.

positions.label: Post-petition appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the broad definition of 'property of the estate' under § 541(a) means that post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Post-petition appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) limits the converted estate to property as of the original filing date, meaning post-petition appreciation belongs to the debtor, not the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may impose sentences at supervised release revocation that are based on punishing the defendant for the violation, as opposed to sanctioning the breach of trust or addressing the factors in 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the permissible purposes of revocation sentences under supervised release. Some circuits allow courts to expressly punish defendants for their violations, while others hold that revocation sentences should focus on the breach of trust and not serve as additional punishment for the underlying violation conduct. The Sixth Circuit's precedent in United States v. Lewis is at the extreme of this split.

positions.label: Punishment for violations is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences that punish the defendant for the violation of supervised release conditions.

positions.label: Revocation sentences should not be punitive
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of supervised release revocation is to sanction the breach of the court's trust and that revocation sentences should not serve as punishment for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: The circuits are divided on whether compassionate release motions may encompass claims that overlap with habeas corpus relief — such as legal errors at trial or sentencing — or whether such claims must be channeled exclusively through § 2255. This affects prisoners who may lack an avenue for habeas relief but have potentially meritorious claims of legal error.

positions.label: May consider legal errors in compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider claims of legal error or unfairness in the original conviction or sentence as factors in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: May not consider legal errors in compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that claims challenging the validity of a conviction or sentence must be brought through § 2255 and cannot serve as the basis for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA creates a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits have held that RLUIPA, enacted under the Spending Clause, does not clearly authorize personal-liability damages against individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds, while others have allowed such claims to proceed.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA provides a cause of action for money damages against state prison officials sued in their individual capacities for violations of prisoners' religious exercise rights.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials because Congress cannot impose personal liability on non-recipient individuals through the Spending Clause.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
